newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says tobacco rules are "moral obligation".
newsitem.headline: Clinton says tobacco rules are "moral obligation".

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton hailed the new national crackdown on teen smoking on Friday as a "moral obligation" and said the controversial initiative reflects an "instinctive urge" to protect young people from danger.

In an unprecedented presidential challenge to the tobacco industry, Clinton has pushed since 1995 for restricting tobacco sales and advertising to youths. He called the fight against teen-age smoking a "moral obligation."
"Most of us have an instinctive urge to protect our young people from danger," Clinton said at a White House ceremony attended by teen-age anti-smoking activists.

"We teach them to look both ways before crossing the street. We tell them not to touch a hot stove. We make sure they bundle up before going out in the cold," he said. "We should wrap that same protective arm around them when it comes to resisting smoking and the advertising and marketing of cigarettes."

The first new regulation, effective on Friday, makes it a federal crime to sell cigarettes or smokeless tobacco to minors and requires retailers to check photo IDs of anyone under age 27. Merchants caught violating the rules face a $250 fine.

Other restrictions on advertising, vending machine and tobacco sponsorship of sporting or entertainment events are to be phased in over the next 18 months -- if they survive a court battle being waged by the tobacco industry.
Clinton noted that teen smoking has risen in the last few years and 3,000 adolescents start smoking each day. The habit is likely to kill one-third of them later in life.
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulations aim to cut the teen-smoking rate in half over seven years.

The new rule went into effect on FDA Commissioner David Kessler's last day on the job. After more than six years as perhaps the most outspoken and controversial FDA commissioner in memory, Kessler resigned to become dean of Yale medical school.

All 50 states and the District of Columbia already outlaw tobacco sales to minors, but the local laws are unevenly enforced. Studies have shown that kids succeed in buying cigarettes nearly 70 percent of the time.
Anna Santiago, a teen activist from Illinois chosen to speak at the White House event, told reporters afterward that the new regulations already are having an effect.
"The kids are quitting because they don't want to go through all the hassle, all the trouble of getting an ID and, you know, making sure that you look 18 or whatever," she said.
Public health groups have embraced the new rules and have said they will start their own enforcement drive to supplement a federal effort that will gear up slowly.

Although no retailer can be fined on the basis of citizen complaints, such reports can trigger an official inspection into instances in which a 15- or 16-year-old accompanied by an authorized adult agent would try to buy cigarettes.
Merchants in violation will get a warning letter, and if they break the rule again during a follow-up official check, they would be fined, FDA enforcement officials have said.
The FDA has sent out letters and brochures to retailers explaining the new rules, and has held town meetings and videoconferences across the country.
